content:
Abraham, the critic says, never came near Arabia, and the story of his building the Kaaba was devised to give Islam a patriarch. On this view the House is a pagan shrine with an Abrahamic label.

This article aims to provide context to that claim, insha'Allah, in five points: what the Quran says, what the hadith add, what Genesis records of Ishmael, what the Meccans themselves claimed, and what the record outside scripture can and cannot show.

"The first House (of worship) appointed for men was that at Bakka: full of blessing and of guidance for all kinds of beings" (3:96).[1]

The Quran gives the account in four places. Abraham and Ishmael raise the foundations of the House and pray that God accept it from them (2:127). God shows Abraham the site and tells him to keep it pure for those who circle it, stand and bow in prayer (22:26).

Abraham prays at the House for the offspring he has settled "in a valley without cultivation" (14:37), and the place where he stood is named as a place of prayer (2:125).

The Quran ties the building to two named prophets, a named site and a named rite. It is a claim made openly, to an audience that knew the House.

The fullest narration is from Ibn Abbas. Abraham leaves Hagar and the infant Ishmael in the valley; the water runs out; Hagar runs between the hills; an angel strikes the ground and Zamzam flows.[2]

Years later Abraham returns and tells Ishmael that God has commanded him to build a House. Ishmael brings the stones, Abraham builds, and both pray, "Our Lord, accept from us" (2:127).[3]

The rites of the pilgrimage keep the story in practice: the running between al-Safa and al-Marwa follows Hagar's steps.

Genesis sends Ishmael south. After Hagar and her son are sent away, Ishmael "lived in the wilderness of Paran, and his mother took a wife for him from the land of Egypt" (Genesis 21:21, ESV).

Abraham did not lose him. At Abraham's death, "Isaac and Ishmael his sons buried him in the cave of Machpelah" (Genesis 25:9, ESV).

Genesis does not mention the Kaaba, and Muslims do not claim it does. It does place Ishmael in the desert to the south, in touch with his father, which is the setting the Quran describes. We set out the rest in Ishmael in the Quran and Genesis.

The Quran made its claim to the people who kept the House. They called themselves the offspring of Ishmael, honoured the sanctuary and performed a pilgrimage there before Islam, and the Quran faulted them for the idols they had set up in it.

When the Prophet (peace be upon him) entered Mecca at the conquest, there were 360 idols around the Kaaba. He struck them down, reciting 17:81.[4] On the Quran's account this was a restoration: the House returned to the worship of the One God for which Abraham built it.

We set out what the Meccans believed in What the pagans of Mecca said about Allah.

The record outside scripture is thin. A Greek historian of the first century BC describes a temple in western Arabia "revered by all Arabians", and the identification with the Kaaba is possible and unproven. We weigh that and four other witnesses in The Kaaba before Islam: 5 ancient witnesses, weighed.

No archaeology of Abraham exists anywhere, in Hebron, Ur or Mecca. The silence that the critic finds in Arabia is the same silence that surrounds the patriarch in Canaan, and the critic does not conclude from it that Genesis invented Hebron.

Strength: moderate. The account rests on revelation. The historical record leaves it standing.

The bottom line

The Quran names the builders, the site and the rites; the hadith of Ibn Abbas give the story; Genesis places Ishmael in the southern desert in contact with his father; the Meccans claimed his descent; and the outside record is silent in Arabia as it is in Canaan.

The claim of invention needs evidence of its own, and it has none. "Our Lord! Accept (this service) from us" (2:127). Allah knows best.

Notes

  1. Quran 3:96, A. Yusuf Ali translation.
  2. Sahih al-Bukhari 3364, report of Ibn Abbas.
  3. Sahih al-Bukhari 3365, report of Ibn Abbas.
  4. Sahih al-Bukhari 4287, report of Abdullah ibn Mas'ud.
